entries.definition: Chemical-family grouping of the filament's base polymer (polylactide, copolyester, styrenic, polyamide, elastomer, etc.).
entries.why_it_matters: Materials in the same class share printing behavior, bonding compatibility, and post-processing options. It is the primary axis for filtering and for predicting whether two materials will fuse.

entries.definition: Hotend temperature range the material extrudes reliably at, with a single most-recommended value.
entries.why_it_matters: Too cold causes under-extrusion and weak layer bonds; too hot causes stringing, oozing, and polymer degradation. The recommended value is the consensus starting point before tuning.

entries.definition: Build-plate temperature range for first-layer adhesion and warp control.
entries.why_it_matters: Keeps the part above/near its glass transition at the interface so it grips the plate. Wrong bed temps are the top cause of failed first layers and elephant's foot.

entries.definition: Recommended air temperature surrounding the print.
entries.why_it_matters: High-shrinkage materials (ABS, ASA, PA, PC) need warm, draft-free air to cool evenly; printing them in a cold room guarantees warping and layer splitting.

entries.definition: Volumetric-flow-limited linear speed range the material prints well at on typical hardware.
entries.why_it_matters: Every polymer has a melt rate; exceeding it causes under-extrusion. Flexibles and high-temp materials generally need slower speeds than PLA/PETG.

entries.definition: Whether a passive enclosure measurably improves results for this material.
entries.why_it_matters: Enclosures block drafts and retain heat, reducing warp and layer splitting. Also relevant for containing VOCs/particulates from styrenics.

entries.definition: Whether an actively heated chamber (not just an enclosure) is effectively mandatory for usable parts.
entries.why_it_matters: True high-performance polymers (PEEK, PEI/ULTEM, PPS) delaminate without 60–150 °C chamber temps; this flag separates 'hobbyist-printable' from 'industrial-hardware' materials.

entries.definition: Whether the filament abrades brass nozzles (carbon/glass fiber, metal, glow additives).
entries.why_it_matters: Filled filaments can destroy a brass nozzle in a single spool; hardened steel, ruby, or carbide is required.

entries.definition: Recommended dehydration temperature and duration before printing.
entries.why_it_matters: Hygroscopic polymers absorb atmospheric moisture that boils in the hotend, causing popping, stringing, foaming, weak parts, and rough surfaces. Nylon and PVA can become unprintable in hours of exposure.

entries.definition: Observable signs that filament is properly dried and preparation was sufficient.
entries.why_it_matters: Drying blind wastes time or under-dries. Checks include: no audible popping or visible steam while extruding, no foamy/matte extrudate, minimal stringing on a retraction test, and weight-loss plateau between drying cycles.

entries.definition: How aggressively the material absorbs moisture from air (low / moderate / high / extreme).
entries.why_it_matters: Determines storage rigor: 'low' tolerates open-air storage for weeks; 'extreme' (PVA, PA) needs dryboxes with desiccant and printing from a dryer.

entries.definition: Percentage the polymer contracts as it cools from extrusion to room temperature.
entries.why_it_matters: Drives warping, dimensional error, and internal stress. Parts needing tight fits must be compensated by this factor in CAD or slicer.

entries.definition: Mass per unit volume of the solid polymer.
entries.why_it_matters: Converts spool weight to printable volume, estimates part weight, and affects cost-per-part. Basis for the standardized weight-per-volume and volume-per-weight figures.

entries.definition: Standardized mass of 100 cm³ of solid material (density × 100).
entries.why_it_matters: Lets you compare 'how heavy will this part be' across materials at a glance.

entries.definition: Standardized solid volume yielded by 100 g of material (100 ÷ density).
entries.why_it_matters: Lets you compare 'how much part does a spool buy' across materials — lightweight polymers like PP yield notably more volume per spool.

entries.definition: Temperature at which the amorphous polymer softens from rigid to rubbery.
entries.why_it_matters: Practical ceiling for structural use — parts sag and creep near Tg. Explains why PLA fails in a parked car (~60 °C) and ASA does not.

entries.definition: Temperature at which a standard bar deflects under a standard load (0.45 MPa unless noted).
entries.why_it_matters: The load-bearing analogue of Tg; the better number for 'will this bracket survive under load at temperature'.

entries.definition: Highest continuous-use temperature at which printed parts retain useful properties.
entries.why_it_matters: The single number to check for under-hood, near-hotend, or hot-environment applications.

entries.definition: A composite expert score of how forgiving the material is on ordinary hardware with default profiles. It is not a single measurement: it aggregates seven weighted factors — (1) hardware gating: what the material refuses to print without (enclosure, heated chamber, all-metal hotend, hardened nozzle, special build surface, direct-drive extruder, feeding assistant); (2) moisture burden: how aggressively it must be dried and kept dry to print at all; (3) first-layer & warp management: adhesion aids, brims, and draft sensitivity needed to keep parts attached and flat; (4) tuning-window width: how narrow the workable temperature/speed/cooling windows are and how badly results degrade outside them; (5) failure-mode frequency: how often prints fail (clogs, delamination, corner lift, jams) even for experienced users; (6) speed ceiling: how far below common printing speeds the material forces you; (7) repeatability: once dialed in, whether it stays dialed in. Each entry is scored against the fixed anchors — PLA=10, PETG=7, ASA=5, unfilled PA / soft TPU=3, PEEK-class=1 — and every entry scores independently: a variation or grade (TPU 95A vs 60A, PLA vs LW-PLA, PA6-CF vs PA12) gets its own score because these factors genuinely differ between grades.
entries.why_it_matters: Predicts time-to-success and whether special hardware or process discipline is needed before you buy a spool. Because it is a composite, check the entry's printing/drying/feeding sections to see WHICH factor is dragging a low score — a 3 driven by moisture (PVA) is a different problem than a 3 driven by hardware gating (PC).

rubric.10: Prints reliably on any machine, open frame, minimal tuning (PLA)
rubric.9: PLA-like process with one extra care item, e.g. moisture (PVB)
rubric.7: Minor tuning; watch moisture or stringing (PETG)
rubric.5: Needs enclosure or careful tuning; failures common without (ABS, HIPS)
rubric.3: Needs drybox, slow speeds, direct drive, or special surfaces (PA, TPU 85A)
rubric.2: Multiple simultaneous barriers, incl. build-surface chemistry (PP)
rubric.1: Industrial hardware and expertise required (PEEK, PEI/ULTEM)

entries.definition: Whether the material feeds through any extruder ('any'), works notably better with the extruder gears directly above the hotend ('direct-drive-recommended'), or effectively cannot be pushed through a long Bowden tube at all ('direct-drive-required').
entries.why_it_matters: Flexible filament under compressive load buckles inside a Bowden tube like pushing rope — the softer the grade, the shorter the unsupported path must be. TPU ≥95A can survive a short Bowden; ~85A-90A wants direct drive; ≤85A demands it. Rigid materials feed through anything.

entries.definition: Whether the filament is safe to load in automatic material systems (Bambu AMS/AMS 2/AMS HT, Prusa MMU, Creality CFS): 'yes', 'conditional' (works with specific precautions or specific units), or 'no'.
entries.why_it_matters: AMS units push filament through long PTFE paths with rubber rollers — soft flexibles (TPU 90A and below) buckle and jam them, which is why vendors bar them; firm grades around ~55D-64D (e.g. Bambu TPU for AMS at 68D, TPU 60D-class) feed fine. Brittle materials (damp PVA, some filled filaments) can snap inside the feed path, and abrasive filaments wear the PTFE. A jam mid-multi-color-print usually kills the print, so check this before assigning a material to an AMS slot rather than an external spool holder.

entries.definition: Whether soft grades benefit from a powered or gravity-assist feeder that moves filament from the spool to the extruder inlet so the extruder never pulls against spool drag.
entries.why_it_matters: Very soft filament (~60A-85A) stretches under the tension of unwinding its own spool, causing under-extrusion that no extruder setting fixes. A spool-side assistant (motorized unwinder, low-friction top-mount, or short guided path) removes that tension. Mostly irrelevant at 95A and above.

entries.definition: Indentation hardness of elastomers and soft polymers, measured on the Shore A scale (softer, rubber bands ~20A, skateboard wheels ~95A) or Shore D scale (harder; ~55D-64D overlaps the top of the A scale and behaves semi-rigid). Filament grades are named by it: TPU 85A, 90A, 95A, 60D.
entries.why_it_matters: For flexibles this single number drives nearly everything: printability (harder = easier), drive-system and AMS requirements, feeding-assistant need, print speed ceiling, and part behavior (energy return, grip, compression set). Two 'TPU' spools at 60A and 60D are, in practice, different materials — which is why each grade gets its own catalog entry rather than sharing one.

entries.definition: On an enclosed printer, whether this material prints better with the door/lid open so ambient heat escapes.
entries.why_it_matters: The inverse of the enclosure requirement: low-Tg materials (PLA, PVB) and heat-soft flexibles deform, string, and clog from heat creep inside a 35-45 °C sealed chamber. Enclosed printers routinely warn to open the door for PLA. Materials with this flag true pair badly with 'set and forget' enclosed printing of mixed-material jobs.

entries.definition: Recommended part-cooling fan duty range while printing (percent of full speed).
entries.why_it_matters: Cooling is a per-material trade: high cooling sharpens detail and overhangs but weakens layer bonds. PLA wants ~100%; PETG ~30-50%; ABS/ASA/PC nearly none (cooling splits their layers); flexibles vary by grade. The recommended value is the profile starting point.

entries.definition: How precisely printed dimensions match design and hold over time (creep, moisture swell, thermal drift).
entries.why_it_matters: Critical for functional parts with tolerances: enclosures, gears, press fits, printer parts.

rubric.10: Holds sub-0.1 mm accuracy and shape over years indoors
rubric.5: Noticeable creep under sustained load or moisture-driven swelling
rubric.1: Distorts readily with heat, load, or humidity

entries.definition: How strongly the material lifts corners and distorts while printing. Higher = warps MORE (inverted scale).
entries.why_it_matters: Warping scales with part footprint; a high score means large flat parts need brims, enclosures, and adhesion strategy.

rubric.1: Essentially never warps (PLA on any surface)
rubric.5: Warps on large parts without enclosure (PETG large flats)
rubric.10: Unprintable at size without heated chamber (PP, PEEK, unfilled PA)

entries.definition: Relative strength of the bond between printed layers versus the material's bulk strength — scored on the measured Z-to-XY strength ratio where data exists, not on subjective toughness. Note for elastomers: TPU/TPE score low here (Z/XY ≈ 27-31% by elongation) even though their parts feel tough and rarely snap in casual use — the flexibility masks the anisotropy until a bend loads the layer lines directly. This is a deliberate rubric choice: the score answers 'how much weaker is Z than XY', not 'do parts feel sturdy'.
entries.why_it_matters: FDM parts fail at layer lines first; a material with great tensile specs but poor layer adhesion is weak in practice, especially loaded in Z. For flexibles, orient bends in-plane — a TPU part that flexes beautifully in XY can snap without warning when the same bend loads Z.

rubric.10: Near-isotropic; Z strength close to XY (PCTG, well-printed PETG)
rubric.5: Distinct Z weakness; orient loads in-plane

entries.definition: Resistance to crushing loads relative to other FDM materials.
entries.why_it_matters: Jigs, feet, spacers, and press tools load parts in compression, where FDM parts are strongest — this score ranks materials for those uses.

entries.definition: Composite score for retaining strength and shape at elevated temperature.
entries.why_it_matters: Quick filter for hot environments; see Tg/HDT/max service temp for the underlying numbers.

entries.definition: Resistance to sunlight-induced embrittlement, chalking, and color fade.
entries.why_it_matters: UV degradation is the main killer of outdoor prints; ASA exists specifically to fix ABS's poor score here.

entries.definition: Composite resistance to the full outdoor cycle: UV, rain, humidity, and temperature swings.
entries.why_it_matters: The single filter for 'can this live outside' — garden fixtures, RC parts, housings, signage.

entries.definition: Resistance to property loss from immersion or sustained moisture (absorption, swelling, hydrolysis).
entries.why_it_matters: Nylon parts absorb water and soften/swell; PVA dissolves outright. Matters for marine, plumbing-adjacent, and bathroom uses.

entries.definition: Whether printed parts survive permanent outdoor placement (no / limited / yes), combining UV stability, moisture behavior, and temperature-swing tolerance into one verdict.
entries.why_it_matters: The quick answer to 'can this live outside'. 'Limited' means seasonal or sheltered use (PETG fades and softens over years of sun); 'yes' means the material was formulated for weather (ASA). Check uv_tolerance and weather_tolerance for the underlying scores, and remember dark colors absorb more heat — a 'limited' material in black on a hot roof fails faster.

entries.definition: Whether parts keep their shape and useful strength in hot environments (no / moderate / yes), anchored to glass transition, HDT, and max service temperature.
entries.why_it_matters: The filter for hot cars, enclosures near electronics, under-hood parts, and anything close to a heat source. 'No' fails in a parked car (~60-70 °C interior); 'moderate' handles that but not sustained engine-bay or near-hotend duty; 'yes' is the PC/PPA/high-performance tier. The numbers behind the verdict live in glass_transition_c, heat_deflection_c, and max_service_temp_c.

entries.definition: The stress at which the material yields or breaks when pulled, in megapascals (MPa). Recorded as a range because published values vary by brand, test method (yield vs break), and print orientation — FDM parts measured along the layers (XY) are markedly stronger than across them (Z).
entries.why_it_matters: The headline number for load-bearing design — how much pull a bracket, hook, or clip takes before failing. Two cautions: datasheet values usually describe injection-moulded or XY-printed specimens, so real Z-loaded prints deliver a fraction of it (see layer adhesion); and a strong-but-brittle material (PLA) fails differently than a weaker-but-ductile one (PETG), so pair this with the compression and layer-adhesion scores rather than reading it alone.

entries.definition: For each filament, a short curated list of other catalog materials worth evaluating instead, each with the specific trade-off reasoning (easier printing, lower cost, better UV, higher temperature ceiling...).
entries.why_it_matters: Material selection is comparative: the right question is rarely 'is ABS good' but 'is ABS better than ASA for this part'. These are directional suggestions — ASA appears as an easier-printing alternative to ABS, while ABS appears as a cheaper alternative to ASA — grounded in the catalog's own scores, prices, and suitability data.

entries.definition: Whether the material can be used for food-contact items (no / conditional / yes on certified lines).
entries.why_it_matters: Even food-safe polymers become unsafe as FDM prints: layer crevices harbor bacteria, and nozzles/additives contaminate. 'Conditional' means certified filament plus sealing or single-use.

entries.definition: Fitness for sustained structural loads (no / light / moderate / high), accounting for creep.
entries.why_it_matters: Short-term strength misleads: PLA is strong but creeps under constant load; PC and filled nylons hold. Use this for brackets, mounts, and fixtures.

entries.definition: Other filament types that weld to this one when co-printed in multi-material prints.
entries.why_it_matters: Enables multi-material design (flex+rigid, soluble supports) and predicts which combinations delaminate at the interface.

entries.definition: Materials usable as support or as a support-interface layer for this filament — either soluble (PVA, BVOH) or cleanly separable (PETG under PLA, HIPS under ABS). HARD RULE: a material is never its own interface, and no same-family material (same base chemistry, e.g. any PLA variant for any other PLA variant, PA6 for PA12-class) qualifies — same-chemistry pairs weld, which is the opposite of a removable interface. Printing supports in the part's own material is a slicer default that works mechanically, but it is breakaway-with-scarring, not an interface choice, and is deliberately not recorded here.
entries.why_it_matters: The right support pairing gives perfect undersides and makes otherwise-unprintable geometry routine. Listing a welding pair as an interface would send users into supports they cannot remove.

entries.definition: Relative level of volatile organic compounds released while the material is melted and extruded (minimal / low / moderate / high).
entries.why_it_matters: VOCs like styrene (ABS/ASA) and caprolactam (nylon) are respiratory irritants and, for some compounds, suspected carcinogens with chronic exposure. This drives where a printer can safely live — desk, garage, or ventilated cabinet.

entries.definition: Relative level of ultrafine particles (UFP, <100 nm) released during printing.
entries.why_it_matters: UFPs penetrate deep into lungs and are emitted by all FDM printing to some degree — hotter-printing materials generally emit far more. Independent of VOCs: a material can be low-odor but still a high UFP emitter.

entries.definition: Whether ventilation/filtration during printing is optional, recommended, or required for this material.
entries.why_it_matters: The actionable summary of the emissions data: 'optional' suits occasional printing in living spaces, 'recommended' means move air or filter (HEPA+carbon) for regular use, 'required' means never print it in occupied unventilated rooms.

entries.definition: Chemicals, tools, and practices that harm a specific build surface, each with the damage mechanism and a severity: 'destroys' (surface ruined outright), 'degrades' (shortens life or permanently reduces adhesion), 'cosmetic' (appearance only).
entries.why_it_matters: Most plate deaths are self-inflicted: acetone crazes PC and some PEI coatings, metal scrapers gouge powder coat, thermal shock cracks glass and delaminates coated sheets, and aggressive solvents strip adhesive layers. Cleaning habits that are safe on one surface chemistry ruin another — check this list before applying any solvent, tool, or trick learned on a different plate.

entries.definition: Maturity of an entry's data: placeholder, low, medium, or high.
entries.why_it_matters: This catalog is built incrementally by research sessions; confidence tells you whether a number is a consensus of datasheets or a first-pass estimate.
